newsitem.title: MEXICO: FORECAST - Mexico 1996 GDP estimates revised up.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Mexico 1996 GDP estimates revised up.

text.p: Mexico's economy may have grown by as much as 5.0 percent in 1996, powered by strong growth in the fourth quarter, economists said on Tuesday.

The Mexican government's official forecast for 1996 growth in gross domestic product (GDP) is 4.0 percent, but analysts and even goverment officials said it should come in higher than those earlier forecasts.
The GDP figures are set to be released on Wednesday.

"What we are going to see is a slightly diminished base of export growth, strong investment spending, and consumer spending starting to pick up a bit but still fairly modest," Morgan Stanley economist "Chip" Brown said.
Santander Investment has an official forecast of 4.7 percent for fourth quarter GDP, but economist Enrique Ramirez said they now expect a number closer to 6.3 or 6.4 percent for the quarter.
"That means that growth in GDP for the whole year will be close to 5.0 percent," Ramirez said. "This will have a positive impact on the markets," he added.
Recently released industrial production figures point to strong fourth quarter GDP growth.
Industrial production rose 11.2 percent in December over the same month a year earlier, and 10.78 percent for the year, the government said earlier this month.
Brown said Morgan Stanley was looking at fourth quarter industrial GDP growth of around 13.5 percent.

"The point is that manufacturing is coming along well, along with its components," Brown said. "This suggest that construction spending and probably capital goods spending was pretty strong at the tail end of the year," he said.
Domestic demand was weak for most of last year, but is seen gaining strength.

"The implication of an increase in investment spending and and increase in inventories is that there is demand out there somewhere," Brown said. "And very likely it will not be only a fourth quarter event."
Market analysis company IDEA said in a report that it is forecasting a fourth quarter GDP increase of 6.1 percent, leaving 1996 GDP up 4.9 percent year-over-year.

During a recent visit in Switzerland Finance Minister Guillermo Ortiz said that he would not argue with private sector forecasts that were higher than the official government forecast. He had earlier said that preliminary data had shown that GDP had risen by 4.6 to 4.7 percent for the year.

A survey by Reuters of 11 Mexico City offices of brokerages and research firms found average forecasts of 5.25 percent for the fourth quarter.The survey also found expectations of 4.65 percent for the year.
In the third quarter GDP rose by 7.4 percent.
In 1995 GDP fell by a sharp 6.2 percent, after the peso crashed in late 1994 and the economic crisis deepend the year after.
